planting.note: Scatter seed directly onto prepared, shaded canyon-floor or woodland beds in fall so cool-season moisture triggers germination ahead of a late-winter rosette stage and spring bloom.

directions: False dayflower carpets the shaded floor of Edwards Plateau oak-juniper canyons each spring, sending up three-petaled lavender-pink blooms that open briefly in the morning and close by midday. This short-lived Texas native thrives in the dappled light and leaf-litter soils found along limestone canyon walls and spring-fed creek bottoms, reseeding itself freely from year to year once established. Scatter seed directly onto prepared shaded beds in fall so winter moisture can trigger germination ahead of the late-winter rosette stage. It pairs naturally with cedar sage and Texas columbine in a woodland wildflower planting and needs no supplemental fertilizer in reasonably fertile canyon soils.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Plant Database

planting.note: Plant small bulb-like divisions in fall directly into humus-rich, well-drained soil tucked among limestone rocks or at the base of established oaks and junipers where dappled shade persists year-round.

directions: Drummond's woodsorrel is a diminutive Hill Country native that threads through leaf litter on shaded limestone canyon slopes, its clover-like trifoliate leaves topped by small lavender-pink flowers in spring. The plant persists through dry Texas summers via a small underground bulb-like root, going dormant above ground until cool, moist conditions return. Plant divisions or offsets in fall directly into humus-rich, well-drained soil tucked among rocks or at the base of established oaks and junipers for the dappled shade it prefers. Once established it slowly naturalizes into drifts, making it a fitting groundcover companion for maidenhair fern and Hill Country columbine in a canyon-themed native bed.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Plant Database

planting.note: Transplant nursery divisions in fall into well-drained, limestone-derived soil shaded most of the day, watering to establish roots before the plant settles into winter dormancy.

directions: Texas silverpuff forms low rosettes with woolly, silvery undersides that carpet the shaded, leaf-strewn paths of Balcones Canyonlands ashe juniper woodlands, sending up composite flower heads on wiry stems well above the foliage that nod over as they pass into fruit. This evergreen perennial tolerates the deep, dry shade beneath a closed juniper-oak canopy better than most Edwards Plateau wildflowers, spreading gradually by rosette offsets along canyon trails and seep margins. Transplant nursery divisions in fall into well-drained, limestone-derived soil shaded most of the day, watering only to establish roots before winter dormancy. Once settled, it needs little attention beyond occasional removal of spent flower stalks and makes a quietly effective groundcover at the base of Texas mountain laurel or Lindheimer's silktassel.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Plant Database

planting.note: Root cuttings in spring and plant in part shade along a canyon-style limestone wall, fence, or mature tree trunk where the vine can climb without smothering smaller companion plants.

directions: Sevenleaf creeper is a deciduous, tendril-climbing vine endemic to the Edwards Plateau and Lampasas Cut Plain, found scaling limestone canyon walls and riparian tree trunks, with leaflets that vary from five to seven per leaf, overlapping somewhat with the more familiar Virginia creeper it resembles. Small blue-black berries follow inconspicuous summer flowers and feed migrating songbirds through fall, when the foliage turns shades of red and burgundy against the pale limestone. Root cuttings in spring in part shade along a canyon-style rock wall, fence, or mature tree where the vine can climb without smothering smaller companion plants. It tolerates the periodic flooding and heavy shade of bald-cypress-lined creek corridors better than most woody vines, making it well suited to a naturalistic riparian planting.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Plant Database

planting.note: Direct-sow seed in fall onto well-drained, limestone-derived soil under an open oak or juniper canopy; the first-year rosette needs the filtered light and cool-season moisture typical of canyon rims to establish before it bolts and blooms the following spring.

directions: Bracted jewelflower is a Texas endemic found only in the oak-juniper woodlands and canyon rims of a handful of central Hill Country counties, where its slender flowering stalks carry small, bract-cupped maroon-and-cream flowers above a basal rosette. It grows as an annual or biennial, typically spending its first months as a low rosette tucked into thin, rocky, partially shaded soil before bolting and flowering in late winter and spring. Direct-sow seed in fall onto well-drained, limestone-derived soil under an open oak or juniper canopy, since the rosettes need the filtered light and cool-season moisture typical of canyon slopes to establish. Because wild populations are limited and closely tracked by state botanists, garden plantings grown from reputable native seed sources are a meaningful way to support this uncommon Edwards Plateau specialty.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Plant Database

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into a gritty, limestone-based mix tucked between rocks or at the base of a shaded wall, keeping the planting evenly moist only until new fronds emerge.

directions: Ovate-leaf cliffbrake is a robust, evergreen fern rooted in the shaded limestone crevices and canyon walls of the Edwards Plateau, its wiry stems carrying broad, rounded leaflets that distinguish it from the smaller-leaved cliffbrakes sharing its rocky habitat. Unlike many ferns, it tolerates the brief dry spells common to thin, fast-draining canyon soils once its root system has worked into a crack or ledge. Plant divisions in spring directly into a gritty, limestone-based mix tucked between rocks or at the base of a shaded wall, keeping the planting evenly moist only until new fronds emerge. Established plants need minimal care beyond an occasional trim of old fronds and make an excellent companion to Wright's cliffbrake and other native rock ferns in a shaded grotto garden.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Plant Database
